section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Usual Notion of Convergence
section_1.content: Recall the standard real-number metric (Euclidean distance). A series converges if the tail terms get 'small' in terms of absolute value (e.g., 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8... = 1). Visualize this as points moving closer on a number line toward a limit.
section_1.example: A jumping frog moving toward a lily pad: each jump is half the remaining distance; it never 'overshoots'.

section_2.title: Introducing the 2-adic Metric
section_2.content: Define the 2-adic norm |x|_2: for any rational number, |x|_2 = 1/2^k where k is the highest power of 2 dividing x. Crucially, higher powers of 2 are considered 'smaller'. This shifts our perspective: 8 is 'closer' to 0 than 2 is.
section_2.example: Visualizing a 'P-adic tree': branching factor of 2. Nodes at depth 3 (like 8) are 'deeper' (closer to the root 0) than nodes at depth 1 (like 2).

section_3.title: Infinite Sums in the 2-adic World
section_3.content: Apply the convergence criterion: a series converges if the terms 'shrink' in the 2-adic metric. This allows for 'bizarre' sums that diverge in standard math. We use the property that |a + b|_2 ≤ max(|a|_2, |b|_2) (The Ultrametric Inequality).
section_3.example: The sum 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... = -1. Visually, as we add higher powers of 2, the '2-adic distance' to -1 shrinks toward zero.

section_4.title: Application: The Geometry of 'Smallness'
section_4.content: Summarize how changing the definition of 'distance' transforms the landscape of calculus. In the 2-adic world, every triangle is isosceles, and the space is totally disconnected (like a Cantor set).
section_4.example: A data-transmission robot: it experiences 'distance' not by physical meters, but by how many bits of an integer match. Using 2-adic metrics helps optimize error-correcting codes.

        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text("- " + line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
